title: Experiments, Sample Spaces and Counting

intro.x: Probability is a language for describing uncertain outcomes. Before we can assign a number to “how likely”, we must say precisely what can happen. This chapter builds that vocabulary (sample spaces and events), states the classical rule for equally likely outcomes, and develops the counting tools needed to apply it.

blocks.x: A random experiment is a procedure whose result is not determined in advance, but whose set of possible results is known. We do not need the procedure to be repeatable in practice; we only need a clear description of the possible results.
The sample space $\Omega$ is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment. An element $\omega\in\Omega$ is called an outcome.

The sample space must satisfy two requirements. First, it must be exhaustive: every possible result corresponds to some $\omega$. Second, it must be mutually exclusive: two different outcomes cannot occur together in a single run of the experiment.
One coin toss: $\Omega=\{H,T\}$.
One roll of a die: $\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$.
Two rolls of a die, recording both numbers in order: $\Omega=\{1,\dots,6\}^2=\{(i,j):1\le i,j\le 6\}$, with $36$ outcomes.
Tossing a coin until the first head: $\Omega=\{1,2,3,\dots\}=\N$, where $n$ means “the first head occurs on toss $n$”. This set is infinite but countable.
The lifetime of a light bulb in hours: $\Omega=[0,\infty)$. This set is uncountable.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: the sample space is a modelling choice

blocks.x: The same physical experiment can be described by different sample spaces. For two dice we could record the ordered pair $(i,j)$, or only the sum $\{2,\dots,12\}$. Both are valid sample spaces, but they are not equally convenient. A finer description (the ordered pair) always contains the coarser one (the sum is a function of the pair). As we will see in Section 1.3, choosing a sample space whose outcomes are equally likely is often the key step in a solution.

sections.title: Events and the language of sets

blocks.x: We are rarely interested in a single outcome. We want to ask questions such as “is the sum at least 10?” Each such question corresponds to a subset of $\Omega$.
An event is a subset $A\subseteq\Omega$. We say that $A$ occurs if the outcome $\omega$ of the experiment satisfies $\omega\in A$.

For a finite or countably infinite $\Omega$ we allow every subset to be an event. For uncountable $\Omega$ this is not always possible; the precise resolution (a $\sigma$-algebra of events) is given in Chapter 2, and the reason it is necessary is explained in Chapter 15. Until then, “event” means “any subset we can describe”.
Combining events corresponds to combining sets.
The event $\Omega$ always occurs (the certain event) and $\emptyset$ never occurs (the impossible event).
For any events $A_1,A_2,\dots$ (finitely or countably many),

\Bigl(\bigcup_i A_i\Bigr)^c=\bigcap_i A_i^c,
\qquad
\Bigl(\bigcap_i A_i\Bigr)^c=\bigcup_i A_i^c .

We prove the first identity by showing each side is contained in the other. Let $\omega\in(\bigcup_i A_i)^c$. Then $\omega$ lies in no $A_i$, so $\omega\in A_i^c$ for every $i$, that is, $\omega\in\bigcap_i A_i^c$. Conversely, if $\omega\in\bigcap_i A_i^c$, then $\omega\notin A_i$ for every $i$, so $\omega\notin\bigcup_i A_i$. The second identity follows by applying the first to the events $A_i^c$ and taking complements.

A finite or countable collection of events $B_1,B_2,\dots$ is a partition of $\Omega$ if the events are pairwise disjoint ($B_i\cap B_j=\emptyset$ for $i\ne j$) and $\bigcup_i B_i=\Omega$. Exactly one $B_i$ occurs on every run of the experiment.
Historically, probability began with games of chance in which, by symmetry, every outcome was judged equally likely.
Let $\Omega$ be a finite sample space whose outcomes are equally likely. The probability of an event $A\subseteq\Omega$ is
\Prob(A)=\frac{\abs{A}}{\abs{\Omega}} ,
where $\abs{\cdot}$ denotes the number of elements.
Everything depends on the phrase “equally likely”. It is an assumption about the model, justified (or not) by physical symmetry. It is not something the formula can verify.
Take $\Omega=\{1,\dots,6\}^2$, which has $36$ equally likely outcomes. The event “sum equals $7$” is $\{(1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1)\}$, so its probability is $6/36=1/6$.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: equal likelihood on the wrong space

blocks.x: Suppose we toss two fair coins and let $N$ be the number of heads. It is tempting to take $\Omega'=\{0,1,2\}$ and conclude $\Prob(N=1)=1/3$. This is wrong. The three values of $N$ are not equally likely. The four ordered outcomes $HH,HT,TH,TT$ are equally likely, and $N=1$ corresponds to two of them, so $\Prob(N=1)=2/4=1/2$. A famous historical error of exactly this kind is attributed to d’Alembert, who counted two coin tosses as having three equally likely outcomes. The same trap arises when summing two dice and treating the eleven possible sums as equally likely. The remedy: when physical symmetry is the justification, apply it to the finest description in which the objects are distinguishable.

The formula $\abs{A}/\abs{\Omega}$ fails when $\Omega$ is infinite (there is no way to choose a natural number “uniformly”; see Chapter 2), and it is circular as a definition, since “equally likely” already means “equally probable”. In a continuous setting, “choose at random” can be ambiguous: Bertrand’s paradox asks for the probability that a random chord of a circle is longer than the side of the inscribed equilateral triangle, and three natural interpretations of “random chord” give $1/3$, $1/2$ and $1/4$. The paradox shows that the sampling mechanism must be specified. Chapter 2 gives the axiomatic framework that removes the circularity: probability becomes a function satisfying rules, and the classical formula becomes a special case.
With equally likely outcomes, probability reduces to counting. This section develops the standard tools with proofs.
Basic principles

blocks.name: Proposition
blocks.title: Rule of sum and rule of product

blocks.x: Sum rule. If a task can be done in one of $m$ ways or in one of $n$ ways, and no way is counted twice, there are $m+n$ ways.

Product rule. If a procedure has $k$ stages, and stage $i$ can be carried out in $n_i$ ways regardless of the choices made in earlier stages, then the whole procedure can be carried out in $n_1n_2\cdots n_k$ ways.

The sum rule is the statement $\abs{A\cup B}=\abs{A}+\abs{B}$ for disjoint finite sets. For the product rule with two stages, list the choices of stage 1 as $a_1,\dots,a_{n_1}$. For each $a_i$ there are $n_2$ completions, giving $n_2$ distinct pairs $(a_i,\cdot)$. These blocks are disjoint, so the total is $n_1n_2$. Induction on $k$ gives the general case.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: “regardless of earlier choices” means the number, not the set

blocks.x: In stage 2 the available options may depend on stage 1, as long as their count does not. For example, choosing a president and then a vice president from $n$ people gives $n(n-1)$ outcomes: the set of candidates for vice president depends on who is president, but there are always $n-1$ of them.
Permutations and combinations
For an integer $n\ge 0$, $n!=n(n-1)\cdots 2\cdot 1$, with $0!=1$.
The number of ways to arrange $n$ distinct objects in a row is $n!$.
The number of ordered selections of $k$ objects from $n$ distinct objects, without repetition (called $k$-permutations), is
P(n,k)=n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}.
For (ii), apply the product rule: $n$ choices for the first position, $n-1$ for the second (whatever the first was), and so on, down to $n-k+1$ for the $k$th. Part (i) is the case $k=n$.
The number of $k$-element subsets of an $n$-element set is denoted $\binom{n}{k}$ (read “$n$ choose $k$”), for integers $0\le k\le n$. We set $\binom{n}{k}=0$ if $k<0$ or $k>n$.
For $0\le k\le n$,
\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}.

Count the ordered selections of $k$ distinct objects from $n$ in two ways. By Proposition 1.10 there are $n!/(n-k)!$ of them. Alternatively, first choose which $k$-element set is selected ($\binom nk$ ways), then order its elements ($k!$ ways, by Proposition 1.10(i)). By the product rule the count is $\binom nk\,k!$. Equating the two counts and dividing by $k!$ gives the formula.

Two immediate consequences: symmetry, $\binom nk=\binom n{n-k}$ (choosing the $k$ objects to keep is the same as choosing the $n-k$ to discard), and the special values $\binom n0=\binom nn=1$, $\binom n1=n$.
For $1\le k\le n-1$,
\binom nk=\binom{n-1}{k-1}+\binom{n-1}{k}.

Fix one special object $x$ among the $n$. Every $k$-subset either contains $x$ or does not. Those containing $x$ are formed by choosing the other $k-1$ members from the remaining $n-1$ objects: $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ ways. Those not containing $x$ are $k$-subsets of the remaining $n-1$ objects: $\binom{n-1}{k}$ ways. The two cases are disjoint and exhaustive; apply the sum rule.
For real $a,b$ and integer $n\ge 0$,
(a+b)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a^k b^{n-k}.

Write $(a+b)^n=(a+b)(a+b)\cdots(a+b)$ with $n$ factors. Expanding, we choose from each factor either $a$ or $b$, obtaining $2^n$ terms. The term $a^kb^{n-k}$ arises exactly when $a$ is chosen from some set of $k$ of the $n$ factors; there are $\binom nk$ such sets. Collecting terms gives the formula.
For $n\ge 1$: $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk=2^n$ and $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk=0$.
Put $(a,b)=(1,1)$ and $(a,b)=(-1,1)$ in Theorem 1.14.
The first identity also has a direct meaning: a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets, since each element is independently in or out.
For non-negative integers $m,n,r$,
\sum_{k=0}^r\binom mk\binom n{r-k}=\binom{m+n}{r}.

Take a group of $m$ men and $n$ women and count the committees of size $r$. The right side counts all committees. On the left, $k$ is the number of men on the committee: choose them in $\binom mk$ ways and then the $r-k$ women in $\binom n{r-k}$ ways. Summing over $k$ counts every committee once.
Arrangements with repeated objects
Suppose $n=n_1+\dots+n_r$ objects are arranged in a row, where $n_i$ of them are of type $i$, and objects of the same type are indistinguishable. The number of distinguishable arrangements is
\binom{n}{n_1,\dots,n_r}=\frac{n!}{n_1!\,n_2!\cdots n_r!}.

Give each object a unique label, so that there are $n!$ arrangements. Erasing the labels groups arrangements together: two labelled arrangements look the same exactly when one is obtained from the other by permuting labels within each type. For each unlabelled arrangement there are $n_1!\cdots n_r!$ such labelled arrangements (independent relabelling within each type, by the product rule). Hence the number of unlabelled arrangements is $n!/(n_1!\cdots n_r!)$.
For example, the letters of MISSISSIPPI ($1$ M, $4$ I, $4$ S, $2$ P) can be arranged in $\frac{11!}{1!\,4!\,4!\,2!}=34{,}650$ distinguishable ways.
The four sampling schemes
Choosing $k$ items from $n$ distinct items can be done with or without replacement, and the result can be recorded as an ordered list or an unordered collection. The four counts are:

Three of these were derived above ($n^k$ is the product rule with $n$ options at each of $k$ stages). The remaining one, unordered with replacement, is equivalent to counting the number of multisets of size $k$ from $n$ types, and needs a separate argument.
The number of non-negative integer solutions $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ of $x_1+\dots+x_n=k$ is $\binom{n+k-1}{k}$. Equivalently, this is the number of multisets of size $k$ drawn from $n$ types.

A solution says how many items $x_i$ of type $i$ are chosen. Encode it as a row of $k$ stars and $n-1$ bars: write $x_1$ stars, then a bar, then $x_2$ stars, then a bar, and so on, ending with $x_n$ stars. For example, with $n=3,k=4$ the solution $(2,0,2)$ is $\star\star\,|\,|\,\star\star$. This is a bijection between solutions and rows with $k+n-1$ positions, of which exactly $k$ hold stars. A row is determined by the set of positions of the stars, so there are $\binom{n+k-1}{k}$ of them.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: unordered samples are generally not equally likely

blocks.x: When items are drawn one at a time with replacement from $n$ types, the $n^k$ ordered sequences are equally likely, but the $\binom{n+k-1}{k}$ unordered multisets are not. For $n=3$ types and $k=2$ draws, the multiset $\{a,a\}$ arises from one sequence $(a,a)$, whereas $\{a,b\}$ arises from two sequences, $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$. So $\Prob(\{a,a\})=1/9$ but $\Prob(\{a,b\})=2/9$. Applying the classical formula to multisets would be wrong here. (Interestingly, there are physical systems, namely bosons, for which the multisets are equally likely; whether objects are distinguishable is a fact about nature, not a convention of mathematics.)

A poker hand is a $5$-card subset of a $52$-card deck; there are $\binom{52}5=2{,}598{,}960$ equally likely hands. A full house has three cards of one rank and two of another. Count by stages: choose the rank of the triple ($13$ ways), choose which $3$ of its $4$ suits ($\binom43=4$), choose a different rank for the pair ($12$ ways), choose its $2$ suits ($\binom42=6$). Thus
The probability that a $5$-card hand contains exactly two aces: choose the aces ($\binom42=6$) and the other three cards from the $48$ non-aces ($\binom{48}3=17{,}296$):
This is a hypergeometric probability; we will study that distribution in Chapter 5.

In a room of $n$ people, what is the probability that at least two share a birthday? Assume $365$ equally likely birthdays, independent across people (ignoring leap years and seasonal effects). Take $\Omega=\{1,\dots,365\}^n$, which has $365^n$ equally likely outcomes. It is easier to count the complement $N$, “all birthdays distinct”: by the product rule there are $365\cdot364\cdots(365-n+1)$ such outcomes, so

\Prob(N)=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\Bigl(1-\frac k{365}\Bigr),
\qquad
\Prob(\text{some match})=1-\Prob(N).
To see why a small group suffices, use the inequality $1-x\le e^{-x}$ (valid for all real $x$; it holds because $e^{-x}$ is convex and $1-x$ is its tangent line at $x=0$). Applying it to each factor,
\Prob(N)\le\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}e^{-k/365}=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{n(n-1)}{2\cdot 365}\Bigr),

using $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k=n(n-1)/2$. For $n=23$ the exponent is $-506/730$, which is slightly below $-\ln 2$ (because $730\ln 2\approx 505.98<506$). So $\Prob(N)<1/2$ and $\Prob(\text{some match})>1/2$ when $n=23$. The exact value is $\approx 0.507$.

The surprise comes from the number of pairs: there are $\binom{23}2=253$ pairs of people, and each pair matches with probability $1/365$. The expected number of matching pairs is about $253/365\approx 0.69$, which is not small.

Two habits solve a large fraction of elementary counting questions. First, “at least one” events are usually easiest through the complement “none”. Second, when many weakly dependent coincidences are possible, count the number of pairs (or tuples) that could produce one; this tells you the right order of magnitude immediately. Both ideas will be formalised later: the first through the axioms (Chapter 2), the second through linearity of expectation (Chapter 4).
A fair die is rolled twice. List the sample space and find the probability that the second roll is strictly larger than the first.
Prove that $\binom nk=\frac nk\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ for $1\le k\le n$, once algebraically and once by a counting argument (committee with a designated chair).
Prove $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^2=\binom{2n}{n}$ using Vandermonde’s identity.
How many ways are there to seat $n$ people at a round table, if seatings that differ only by rotation are considered the same? Justify your answer.
How many integer solutions satisfy $x_1+x_2+x_3=10$ with every $x_i\ge 2$? (Hint: shift the variables, then use stars and bars.)
Find the probability that a $5$-card hand is a flush (all one suit, including straight flushes).
A password has $8$ characters, each a lowercase letter or digit. Find the probability that a uniformly random password has no repeated character.

In the birthday problem, show that the exact probability of a match is increasing in $n$. Then compute, using the bound in Example 1.21, a value of $n$ guaranteeing a match probability of at least $0.9$.
(Challenge) Prove the multinomial theorem $(x_1+\dots+x_r)^n=\sum\binom{n}{n_1,\dots,n_r}x_1^{n_1}\cdots x_r^{n_r}$, where the sum is over all non-negative integers with $n_1+\dots+n_r=n$.
